content.text: How common is the multi-line import pattern I have experimented with here in EnquiryForm? Do most people just have all imports, no matter how long, on a single line? What's the approach in general to continuation lines in JavaScript/TypeScript by convention?

input.command: git diff --stat src/components/EnquiryForm/EnquiryForm.tsx; echo ---; git diff src/components/EnquiryForm/EnquiryForm.tsx | head -80

content.text:
Rare as a blanket rule. What I see in your diff is that you've extended the project's Mantine-only convention (`import {\n Table,\n} from '@mantine/core'`) to *every* import in the file, including single-specifier ones like `useEffect` from `'react'` — that's the unusual part, not multi-line imports themselves.

The mainstream default (Prettier, which most TS codebases run unmodified) is: single line up to `printWidth` (80 chars typically), and Prettier only breaks to multi-line — one specifier per line, trailing comma — when the line doesn't fit. Nobody hand-writes that decision; it's automatic and length-driven, so short imports like `import { useEffect } from 'react';` almost never get expanded. Style guides like Airbnb don't add rules on top of this; they just defer to the formatter.

Forcing *every* import onto multiple lines regardless of length, as CLAUDE.md mandates for `@mantine/*` and as you've now done here for all imports, is a deliberate deviation from that default. It buys cleaner diffs (adding/removing a specifier touches one line, not a shared line with unrelated specifiers) at the cost of vertical space and scanability. That's a legitimate tradeoff some teams make, but it's a project-specific choice, not an industry norm — most codebases would flag this as excessive noise from Prettier/ESLint's default config.

If you like the result, worth checking whether your CLAUDE.md convention should explicitly extend beyond `@mantine/*` to all imports, or whether this file should be reverted to match the current documented scope.

I want this repo to act as a showcase for my skills and my approach - though in a wider context than TypeScript development. Really it's about keeping up with current approaches and tools and TypeScript was just an obvious vehicle for that. Therefore it probably makes sense not to use any style that comes across as too quirky or avant-garde, not because they're offensive per se but because they distract from that message I'm trying to send.

content.text:
Agreed — that's the right call. The blanket multi-line-everything treatment has no rationale a reader can infer (unlike the `@mantine/*` rule, which is anchored to a documented RSC bug), so it reads as arbitrary or "look what I can format" rather than "current, professional practice." A showcase repo is better served by output that's indistinguishable from what `prettier` + a standard ESLint config would produce — familiar to any reviewer, zero explaining required.

Recommendation: revert the non-Mantine imports back to single-line (Prettier default), keep the documented multi-line rule scoped to `@mantine/*` only as it already is in CLAUDE.md, since that one has a real, citable reason.

You've got 14 files with this pattern applied (`git diff --stat` above). Want me to revert the import formatting in all of them back to single-line for everything except `@mantine/*` specifiers, leaving the rest of each diff (like the `EnquiryForm.tsx` `maw="32rem"` change) untouched?
Write a new Jira ticket to apply the standard Prettier formatting to everything.
Now creating the ticket in project SYS.

input.summary: Apply standard Prettier formatting throughout the codebase
input.description:
Several files have drifted from standard Prettier output — most notably imports being manually broken onto multiple lines (one specifier per line) even when they fit on a single line, which is not standard Prettier behaviour.

The only documented exception is `@mantine/*` imports, which CLAUDE.md deliberately mandates as multi-line to keep diffs clean when specifiers are added/removed — that rule stays as-is.

Everything else should match plain `prettier` output: single line unless it exceeds `printWidth`, in which case Prettier's own wrapping applies.

This repo is intended as a showcase of current, professional TypeScript practice, so formatting should look like standard tooling output rather than a bespoke or idiosyncratic style — nothing here should read as quirky or attention-drawing for its own sake.

Scope:
- Run `npm run lint:fix` (or `prettier --write`) across the repo to normalise formatting.
- Manually review and revert any hand-applied multi-line import formatting outside `@mantine/*` imports.
- Confirm `npm run lint` and `npm run typecheck` pass with zero errors/warnings afterwards.

content.text:
Not Prettier, and not via VS Code either.

**VS Code:** your global `settings.json` sets `[typescript]`/`[javascript]` formatter to `vscode.typescript-language-features` (the built-in TS language server formatter), but this repo's `.vscode/settings.json` explicitly overrides that to `editor.defaultFormatter: null` for JS/TS/JSX/TSX. So in this workspace, no formatter is wired up for format-on-save at all — `editor.codeActionsOnSave` only runs `source.fixAll.eslint`. There's no `esbenp.prettier-vscode` entry anywhere.

**The project itself:** I checked — there's no `prettier` in `package.json` (dependencies or dev), no `.prettierrc`, and no `eslint-plugin-prettier`. No, because I'm likely to adopt Prettier anyway - unless it clashes with ESLint, which I doubt

content.text:
It's not just theoretical — there's real overlap. `eslint.config.mjs` currently sets several formatting rules directly: `semi`, `comma-dangle`, `eol-last`, `operator-linebreak`, plus the whole `typescript-eslint` `flat/stylistic-type-checked` rule set. Those are exactly the category of rule Prettier and ESLint fight over if both are left active — Prettier reformats a line one way, ESLint's rule flags it (or "fixes" it back), and you get autofix churn or a red squiggle that never resolves.

The standard, well-established fix is `eslint-config-prettier`: it doesn't add rules, it only turns off every ESLint rule that overlaps with formatting, so ESLint owns code quality and Prettier owns layout. Worth including that in the ticket's scope now, or adding as a follow-up when you actually adopt Prettier — happy to leave SYS-598 as-is and note it as a dependency, whichever you prefer.
What would be exampkles of the changes made in this codebase if eslint-config-prettier were to be set?

Less dramatic than you might expect — your ESLint config was largely hand-tuned to already match Prettier's defaults, so `eslint-config-prettier` mostly removes redundancy rather than changing visible output. Concretely, in `eslint.config.mjs`:

**Rules it would turn off:**
- `semi: ["error", "always"]` — Prettier also defaults to semicolons, so no diff, just a change of which tool enforces it.
- `comma-dangle: [...always-multiline...]` — Prettier v3's default (`trailingComma: "all"`) produces the same output for anything already wrapped multi-line, so again no visible diff expected.
- `eol-last: ["error", "always"]` — Prettier always adds a trailing newline; redundant.
- `operator-linebreak: ["error", "after"]` — Prettier's own line-breaking algorithm puts binary operators at the end of the line, matching this.
- `react/jsx-wrap-multilines` — Prettier's JSX formatter wraps multi-line JSX in parens the same way this rule does.

**What it wouldn't touch:** everything semantic/code-quality — `import-x/*`, `simple-import-sort/*`, `sonarjs/*`, `promise/*`, `no-console`, `no-restricted-syntax`, the `no-unsafe-*` and other `@typescript-eslint` rules like `prefer-nullish-coalescing` or `consistent-type-assertions`. None of those are layout rules, so `eslint-config-prettier` leaves them alone.

**The more interesting finding:** your config currently has no `indent`, `quotes`, or `max-len` rule at all — I grepped and there's nothing. So indentation and line-wrapping for long expressions aren't enforced by ESLint today; they rely purely on convention and editor tab settings. That means the real effect of adopting Prettier wouldn't be "rules get disabled," it'd be "Prettier starts enforcing consistent indentation/wrapping for the first time" — which is likely to touch far more lines across the repo than the five rules above ever would, including reformatting whichever of those 14 changed files still have inconsistent indentation.

fields.description:
Several files have drifted from standard Prettier output — most notably imports being manually broken onto multiple lines (one specifier per line) even when they fit on a single line, which is not standard Prettier behaviour.

The only documented exception is `@mantine/*` imports, which CLAUDE.md deliberately mandates as multi-line to keep diffs clean when specifiers are added/removed — that rule stays as-is.

Everything else should match plain `prettier` output: single line unless it exceeds `printWidth`, in which case Prettier's own wrapping applies.

This repo is intended as a showcase of current, professional TypeScript practice, so formatting should look like standard tooling output rather than a bespoke or idiosyncratic style — nothing here should read as quirky or attention-drawing for its own sake.

Note: the project does not currently depend on Prettier at all — no `prettier` package, no `.prettierrc`, no `eslint-plugin-prettier`. Formatting today is enforced only by ESLint (`eslint.config.mjs`), and ESLint has no `indent`, `quotes`, or `max-len` rule, so indentation/wrapping isn't actually linted at present. Adopting Prettier is the intended fix for that gap.

Scope:
- Add `prettier` and `eslint-config-prettier` as dev dependencies, with a `.prettierrc` matching the conventions already documented in CLAUDE.md (single quotes, 4-space indent, etc.).
- Add `eslint-config-prettier` to `eslint.config.mjs` (as the last entry in the config array) to disable ESLint rules that conflict with Prettier's formatting. In the current config this affects: `semi`, `comma-dangle`, `eol-last`, `operator-linebreak`, and `react/jsx-wrap-multilines`. All other rules (import sorting, SonarJS, promise rules, `@typescript-eslint/*` type-aware rules, etc.) are code-quality rules, not formatting, and are unaffected.
- Run `prettier --write .` across the repo to normalise formatting — this is expected to touch indentation and line-wrapping much more broadly than the rule handover above, since ESLint was never checking those.
- Manually review and revert any hand-applied multi-line import formatting outside `@mantine/*` imports.
- Confirm `npm run lint` and `npm run typecheck` pass with zero errors/warnings afterwards.
- Add a `format` / `format:check` npm script and wire it into CI if applicable.
